Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this was introduced to the world by Abraham our father through siring Isaac, actualizing the covenant so that an entire nation from his seed is called "circumcised" through being circumcised at eight days, meaning that from birth and from the womb one surrenders his physical desires unto the Blessed Name; this being the power of contraction (tzimtzum) derived from the Written Torah which fences and channels action.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Deuteronomy, Ha'Azinu 4
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “He encompassed him (yesovevenhu), He instructed him, He guarded him as the apple of His eye” (Deuteronomy 32:10). As taught in Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah 14—‘People say Torah precedes all else, yet I say Israel comes first’—‘He encompassed him’ refers to the surrounding supernal light (ohr makkif) with which the Blessed Name encircles Israel so that no soul can ever be severed from its root.

Wherefore Balaam breached the fences of chastity (Bamidbar Rabbah 20:23), promoting promiscuity, which is termed "falsehood": "Bread of deceit is sweet...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: All elevation and sovereignty in the world occur through the Torah, as it is written: "By me kings reign" (Proverbs 8:15); even the kings of the gentile nations possess a reflection of biblical holiness through the esoteric mystery of the exile. For in truth, if one says: there is Torah among the gentiles—do not believe it (Eichah Rabbah 2:9), for "He has not dealt so with any nation" (Psalms 147:20).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 47:4–5
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And just as this process operates within the physical garment of nature: when clouds obscure the light of the sun, rain and bountiful harvest follow in their wake, as it is written (Psalms 147:8): “Who covers the heaven with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bamidbar Rabbah 20:23: ‘“The people began to engage in harlotry with the daughters of Moav” – come and see what is written upon their exodus from Egypt: “Speak to the children of Israel, and they will return and encamp before Pi HaḤirot” (Exodus 14:2).What is Pi HaḤirot? It is a place designated for harlotry. Because they conducted themselves chastely, it was called Pi HaḤirot. But these, who abandoned themselves to the men, it is written “the people began to engage in harlotry [with the daughters of Moav].” “The people began” – every place that it says “the people,” it is an expression of denigration, but everywhere that it says “Israel,” it is an expression of praise. “The people were as complainers” (Numbers…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bamidbar Rabbah 20:23) to illuminate his argument here (“Wherefore Balaam breached the fences of chastity (Bamidbar Rabbah 20:23), promoting promiscuity, which is termed "falsehood": "Bread of deceit is sweet to a man..." Proverbs 20:17, being fleeting lust and momentary...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For although impurity is the opposite of purity and holiness, and from the side of revelation in this world it appears that impurity “removes” holiness — that is [only] from the side of this “world of falsehood”; but Israel, “seed of truth,” recognize the truth: that it is impossible for anything to exist without the power of Hashem that enlivens it.

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “Speak to the children of Israel … a man or woman who commits any of the sins that men commit ….” (Bamidbar, 5:6)The sin mentioned is stealing from a convert who dies before compensating him for the loss (see Rashi on Bamidbar 5:8). Here it appears that teshuva (repentance) is of no use., 219b) writes, “Rabbi Yehuda said, there is no sin in the world for which there is no teshuva (repentance) to rectify it except for this, and and there is no evil one who cannot see the face of the Shechina except for one who does this, as it is written (Yeshaya, 60:21), “and Your people are all righteous .…”

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For he was called "ruddy, with beautiful eyes," meaning he sheds blood only with the sanction of the Sanhedrin, since bloodshed is not in his inner nature at all, appearing so only externally]. And therefore Mashiach ben David stems specifically from Ammon and Moab [unlike Mashiach ben Yosef who does not descend from Edom], for with him the holy rectification of desire must remain permanently established even in the World to Come, as noted above.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Deuteronomy, Eikev 5
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And at Taberah, and at Massah, and at Kibroth-hattaavah, you provoked the Lord to wrath” (Deuteronomy 9:22). Scripture admonishes a person never to boast in self-assurance, saying ‘I have purified my heart,’ but rather to guard his spirit at every moment against three pitfalls: Taberah (the melancholy born of anger), Massah (doubt in Divine providence), and Kibroth-hattaavah (craving superfluous bodily indulgences).
